subject: Mathematics
central_question: How are events represented as subsets of a sample space and how are valid probabilities assigned and combined using axioms?
in_scope_units: Events as subsets of a sample space and the occurrence of an event.
Impossible, sure, simple and compound events.
Algebra of events using complement, union, intersection and difference.
Mutually exclusive, exhaustive, and mutually exclusive and exhaustive events.
Axiomatic approach to probability and valid assignments to sample points.
Probability of an event as the sum of probabilities of its outcomes.
Probability for finite sample spaces with equally likely outcomes.
Addition rule for the event A or B and its mutually exclusive special case.
Complement rule for the event not A.
Applications to coins, dice, cards, committees, arrangements and combinations.
Miscellaneous examples, exercise problems, summary and historical note.
banned_topics: Expectation and variance of random variables

known_pitfalls.claim: An event is a single outcome only.
known_pitfalls.correction: Any subset of the sample space is an event; a one-outcome event is specifically a simple or elementary event.

known_pitfalls.claim: Mutually exclusive events must together cover the sample space.
known_pitfalls.correction: Mutually exclusive means only that their intersection is empty; covering the sample space is the separate condition of exhaustiveness.

known_pitfalls.claim: P(A ∪ B) always equals P(A) + P(B).
known_pitfalls.correction: For general events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); direct addition applies only when A and B are mutually exclusive.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every sample point must have the same probability.
known_pitfalls.correction: The axioms allow unequal assignments as long as each probability lies in [0,1] and the probabilities of all sample points sum to 1.

known_pitfalls.claim: The classical formula favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes works for every experiment.
known_pitfalls.correction: That formula is used when the finite sample points are equally likely.
Since A and A′ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

recommended_example_progression: Begin with the two-coin sample space in Section 14.1 to represent verbal events as subsets.
Use NCERT Example 1 for complement, union, intersection and difference of events.
Use NCERT Examples 2 and 3 to distinguish mutually exclusive and exhaustive events.
Use NCERT Example 4 to test whether probability assignments satisfy the axioms.
Use the pens and two-toss examples in Section 14.2.1 to add sample-point probabilities.
Use NCERT Examples 5–8 for complement, union and equally likely outcomes.
Finish with NCERT Examples 9–12 for arrangements, card combinations and the three-event addition formula.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter contains Exercise 14.1 on events, Exercise 14.2 on probability calculations, and the ten-question Miscellaneous Exercise on Chapter 14.
